note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Install terminate and connect electrical wiring

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before installing a new submain to a workshop, what must the Level 3 electrician confirm first?
options: The load, cable size, protection and route
The colour the workshop walls will be painted
Which trainee is the fastest at pulling cable
The brand of breaker the client likes best

questions.stem: A 220 V clothes dryer is rated 4,840 W. What current does it draw?
Twelve circuits are planned in one small trunking. How does this affect the choice of cable size?
options: Each cable can carry more, so smaller cables will do
It has no effect if the trunking lid is left on
A grouping factor lowers each cable's rating
Only the first and last circuits need a larger size

questions.stem: Why can a cable in a hot roof space under a zinc roof carry less current than the same cable in a cool room?
options: The roof sheets act as a shield and block the current
The sun's light changes the copper into a weaker metal
The roof space has more dust, which adds resistance
The hot air reduces how much heat the cable can lose

questions.stem: A cable is rated 32 A. A grouping factor of 0.8 applies. What is its corrected rating?
Table data gives 18 mV/A/m for a cable. How many volts are lost when it carries 20 A for 25 m?
options: 9 V

questions.stem: On a 220 V circuit the volt drop is 6.6 V. What percentage of the supply is that?
Your calculation shows too much volt drop on a long run. What is the usual fix?
options: Fit a larger breaker at the board end
Use a smaller conductor to save money
Raise the supply voltage at the meter
Use a larger conductor size

questions.stem: On a 110/220 V supply, why are the 110 V circuits shared out between the two lines in the board?
options: To balance the load so neither line is overloaded
So that every 110 V circuit gets a full 220 V supply
So the neutral conductor can be left out of each circuit
So the meter records less energy than is really used

questions.stem: Two 110 V circuits on opposite lines share a neutral. Line 1 carries 20 A and line 2 carries 12 A (both plain resistive loads). About what current flows in the neutral?
options: 8 A
0 A

questions.stem: Two 110 V circuits share one neutral. Why must their lines be on opposite lines with a two-pole or handle-tied breaker?
options: So both circuits can run at 220 V when needed
So the shared neutral can be a much thinner conductor than the lines
So the neutral is not overloaded and both isolate together
So the breaker trips each time a lamp is switched on

questions.stem: During an inspection of a sub-board, you find its neutral bar joined to the metal case. What is the risk?
options: The sub-board will use more power than before
The breakers in the sub-board will no longer reset after tripping
The neutral bar will become too hot to touch
Normal neutral current flows on earth paths and metalwork

questions.stem: What must the breaker protecting a circuit be matched to?
options: The cable's current rating after correction
The largest breaker that fits the board
The total power of the whole building
The colour of the cable's outer sheath

questions.stem: A GFCI protecting a kitchen counter trips each time an old kettle is used. What should you do?
options: Replace the GFCI with an ordinary breaker
Test the kettle for an earth fault first
Tape the GFCI's test button down
Plug the kettle into an extension lead

questions.stem: An aluminium submain is to be terminated. What must be checked on the terminals?
options: That they are the same colour as the cable sheath
That they were made and marked only for copper conductors here
That they are rated for aluminium, with the right compound
That they are painted to stop any rust forming

questions.stem: Where the maker advises it, why are large lug terminations checked again for tightness after a period in service?
options: Because the lugs change colour as they age
So the client can see the electrician at work
Because the breaker labels need replacing
Conductors can settle and the joint can loosen

questions.stem: When an armoured cable is terminated, what must be done with its steel wire armour?
options: Clamp it in the gland so it is earthed
Cut it off well short of the gland
Bend it back and tape it to the sheath
Twist it into the neutral terminal

questions.stem: Why must the gap round a cable that passes through a fire-rated wall be sealed?
options: So the cable does not move about inside the hole later
So fire and smoke cannot spread through the hole
So insects cannot get into the next room
So the wall looks neat for the painters

questions.stem: In one control panel, why must 220 V power wiring and 24 V control wiring be kept apart, or all insulated for the higher voltage?
options: So the control wires look neater in the trunking
So the panel can be smaller and cheaper to build
So a fault cannot put mains voltage on control wiring
So the power cables do not get warm from the control wires

questions.stem: Why is there a limit to how many cables can go into one conduit?
options: So the conduit is lighter to carry and fix
So fewer conduit fittings need to be bought for the job
So the cables can be different colours
So cables pull in without damage and stay cool

questions.stem: Which product should be used to help pull cables through a long conduit run?
options: A pulling lubricant made for the cable
Dish soap mixed with a little water
Engine oil poured into the conduit
Grease from the workshop's grease gun

questions.stem: When conductors are dressed into a board, why should they not be laid across the busbars or other breakers?
options: So the board cover can be fitted more quickly
So each can be traced and worked on without disturbing others
So the conductors can all be cut much shorter to save copper on the job
So the busbars can be seen through the cover

questions.stem: How should the neutrals of new circuits be connected to the neutral bar?
options: Two or three twisted into the nearest terminal
All joined in one connector beside the bar
In the order of their breakers, one per terminal
Anywhere on the bar, as long as each one is tight enough

questions.stem: Why should each conductor in a board be marked with its circuit number?
options: So the board looks complete and tidy to the inspector
So the client can count the circuits easily
So the conductors can be shortened later
So faults are traced and circuits isolated correctly

questions.stem: Testing a new lighting circuit, you find the lamp holder still live with the switch off. What is the likely fault?
options: The switch is wired in the neutral
The lamp is the wrong wattage
The breaker is the wrong size
The earth conductor is too long

questions.stem: Before an insulation resistance test, what must be done with electronic equipment and dimmers on the circuit?
options: Leave them on so they are tested as well
Disconnect them so the test cannot harm them
Turn them to full brightness for the test
Cover them with a cloth to keep them cool

questions.stem: An insulation resistance reading on a new circuit is far lower than expected. What is the likely cause?
options: The test leads are longer than usual
The breaker was left switched to the off position during the test
Damaged insulation, damp, or equipment left connected
The circuit is too short to give a reading

questions.stem: Why is earth continuity tested at every outlet on a circuit, not only the first one?
options: So the test takes longer and the job is paid at a higher rate
So the tester's battery is used up evenly
Because the first outlet is always earthed
A break anywhere leaves outlets beyond it unearthed

questions.stem: In which order should a new circuit be tested?
options: Dead tests first, then live tests
Live tests first, then dead tests
Only live tests are needed
Any order the tester prefers

questions.stem: Why must live tests be done only after the dead tests have passed?
options: So the tester's battery lasts longer
So a dangerous fault is found before it is energised
So the client is not charged for any of the dead tests done
So the breaker has time to warm up first

questions.stem: A trainee has terminated a conductor with bare copper showing outside the terminal. What should you do?
options: Wrap the bare copper with tape and leave it
Leave it, as the cover will hide the copper
Have him re-terminate it with no bare copper showing
Cut the conductor shorter while it is still connected

questions.stem: During first fix, a trainee runs a cable at an angle across a wall to reach a box. Why is this wrong?
options: Angled runs use far too little cable for the circuit they feed
The plaster will not stick over an angled cable
Angled cables are harder to pull out later
Hidden cables must run straight, where people expect them

questions.stem: Plasterers will cover the walls tomorrow. What must be done today?
options: Finish and inspect first fix, and record the routes
Fit all the outlets and switches on their boxes
Remove the boxes so the plaster goes on flat
Switch on the new circuits to test them live

questions.stem: Why are the drawings updated to show the installation as it was actually built?
options: So the job looks bigger to the client
So later workers know where cables really run
So the price can be raised after the job
So the original design can be thrown away

questions.stem: The government electrical inspector finds a defect in a new installation. What happens next?
options: The power company connects it anyway, with a note
The electrician signs a letter saying it is fine
It is put right and inspected again before connection
The client may connect it themselves if they wish

questions.stem: What should be given to the client when a new installation is handed over?
options: Only the bill for the work and materials
The spare cable and fittings from the job
The keys to the distribution board's lock and the store room
Test results, a circuit chart and as-built details

questions.stem: Which boxes and accessories should be used for outlets on an outside wall that gets rain?
options: Weatherproof ones with a suitable rating
Indoor ones fixed under the window sill
Indoor ones with tape round the plate
Any type, if the cable is sheathed

questions.stem: A house is close to the sea in Negril. What extra care is needed with outdoor terminations?
options: Use bare copper so salt can be seen easily
Corrosion-resistant fittings and sealed enclosures
Leave the box covers off so that any salt can dry out in the sun
Fit the outlets lower down, near the ground

questions.stem: Where a buried cable rises out of the ground and up a wall, how should it be protected?
options: With paint on the sheath where it rises
By planting shrubs round it so it is hidden
In a conduit or guard up to a safe height
It needs no protection once out of the trench

questions.stem: Why is the connection to the earth rod made with a proper clamp and left where it can be inspected?
options: So the rod can be pulled up and reused later
So the client can see that one was fitted
So the clamp can be painted every year
So it stays tight and can be checked over time

questions.stem: A sheathed cable's sheath has been stripped back too far, so single cores show outside the box. What is the fix?
options: Re-terminate so the sheath enters the box
Wrap the bare cores in insulating tape
Push the cores into the wall behind the box
Paint the cores so they look like sheath

questions.stem: Why must both lines of a 220 V circuit be isolated together?
options: So the breaker handle is easier to lock
Either line alone can still give 110 V to earth
So the neutral can carry the full current
So the circuit uses less power when off

questions.stem: You must connect a new circuit into a board that feeds an occupied office. What is the safest approach?
options: Connect it live while the office keeps working
Switch off only the breaker that will feed the new circuit, then start
Agree a shutdown, then isolate and prove the whole board dead
Ask the office staff to hold the cover open

questions.stem: During the final inspection you find a junction box buried behind plaster. What should be done?
options: Leave it, as the circuit tests correctly
Mark its place on the wall with a pencil
Note it on the drawing and close the job
Make it accessible, as joints must be reachable

questions.stem: After all the tests pass, when is a new circuit switched on for the first time?
options: When the person in charge confirms all are clear
As soon as the last terminal is tightened
While the trainees are still fitting covers
Whenever the client asks for the power

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A 220 V air-conditioning unit is rated 2,640 W. What current does it draw, in amps?
A cable is rated 40 A, and a correction factor of 0.7 applies. What is its corrected rating, in amps?
A run has a volt drop of 4.4 V on a 220 V supply. What percentage of the supply is that?
What is the name of the test that proves line, neutral and earth are connected to the right terminals and that switches are in the line?
What is the name of the material used to seal the hole where a cable passes through a fire-rated wall?
What is the name of the fitting that clamps and seals an armoured cable where it enters an enclosure?
Inside a board, on which part do the neutral conductors of all the final circuits end? Give its name.
Table data gives 9 mV/A/m for a cable. The circuit current is 24 A and the run is 40 m. Work out the volt drop, in volts.
What name is given to the correction factor used when a cable runs through a space hotter than its table assumes?
What is the name of the long metal rod driven into the ground to connect an installation to earth?
What is the name of the conductor that joins metal water or gas pipes to the main earth terminal?
Which conductor of a circuit is usually connected first when terminating, and disconnected last?
Which instrument measures the current in a conductor by closing its jaws round it, without disconnecting anything?
What is laid in the trench above a buried cable to warn anyone digging later?
A 220 V circuit may have a volt drop of no more than 3%. How many volts is that?

essays.stem: Describe how you would select the cable size and the protective device for a new 220 V circuit to a 4 kW appliance 35 m from the board. Show the steps and the factors you consider.
essays.modelAnswer: First I work out the design current: 4,000 W ÷ 220 V is about 18.2 A. I choose the next standard breaker size above this, for example 20 A, as long as the maker allows it for the appliance. The cable's rating after correction must be at least the breaker rating. I find the installation method and conditions: how the cable is fixed, whether it runs in a hot roof space, through insulation or bunched with other cables, and apply the correction factors from the tables. I pick a cable size whose corrected rating is 20 A or more. Then I check the volt drop: using the table's mV per amp per metre for that size, multiplied by 18.2 A and 35 m, and make sure it is within the allowed percentage of 220 V. If not, I choose a larger size. Finally I record the choice and the working.
markingPoints: Design current worked out correctly (about 18.2 A)
Breaker chosen at or above the design current
Correction factors for method, heat and grouping applied
Volt drop checked with the table data and length
Larger size if needed; working recorded

essays.stem: Explain how you would share single-phase loads across the two lines of a 110/220 V supply, and the danger of a shared neutral that is wired wrongly.
essays.modelAnswer: In a 110/220 V supply each line is 110 V to neutral and the two lines are 220 V apart. I list the 110 V circuits with their expected loads and put them on alternate lines in the board, so the current on each line is about the same. Large 220 V loads use both lines, so they do not upset the balance. When the lines are balanced, the neutral carries only the difference between them, so it stays cool and the voltages stay steady. If two circuits share one neutral, their lines must be on opposite lines, with a two-pole or handle-tied breaker. If both lines are wrongly put on the same line, the neutral carries the sum of both currents, which can overload and overheat it without any breaker tripping. A broken shared neutral can also put uneven voltages on equipment and damage it.
markingPoints: Explains 110 V line-to-neutral and 220 V line-to-line
Lists loads and alternates circuits for balance
Neutral carries the difference when balanced
Shared neutral: opposite lines and two-pole or tied breaker
Danger: neutral overload, and damage from a lost neutral

essays.stem: Describe how to terminate an armoured submain cable into a distribution board, from preparing the cable to the final checks.
essays.modelAnswer: The supply to the submain is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after, and the board is also dead. I measure the length needed to reach the terminals neatly and mark where the armour will be cut. I remove the outer sheath, then cut the armour wires to length without nicking the inner sheath. I fit the gland parts in the right order, spread the armour over the gland cone and tighten the gland so the armour is clamped and earthed, with a shroud over it. I fit the gland to the board with a locknut and earth tag as required. Inside, I strip the inner sheath, dress the cores neatly, strip and fit lugs or ferrules with the right tool, and connect them to the right terminals at the maker's torque. Finally I check the gland, tightness, identification and test the cable.
markingPoints: Safe isolation with tester checked before and after
Sheath and armour cut to length without damage
Gland fitted so the armour is clamped and earthed
Cores dressed, lugs or ferrules fitted, terminals torqued
Final checks and tests

essays.stem: Describe the inspection and dead tests you would carry out on a newly installed circuit, in order, and say what each one proves.
essays.modelAnswer: First, with the circuit isolated, I carry out a visual inspection: correct cable size and type, cables supported and protected, sheaths entering boxes, terminations tight with no bare copper, correct breaker, and labels in place. Then the dead tests. Continuity of the protective (earth) conductor at every point proves each outlet and metal part is connected to earth, so a fault will trip the breaker. Insulation resistance, usually at 500 V DC with sensitive equipment disconnected, proves there is no breakdown or damage between conductors or to earth. Polarity proves the line goes to the right terminals and that switches and single-pole devices are in the line, not the neutral. Only when all of these pass is the circuit energised for live tests, such as the GFCI trip test. All readings go on the test sheet.
markingPoints: Visual inspection first, with examples
Earth continuity and what it proves
Insulation resistance (test voltage, equipment disconnected) and what it proves
Polarity and what it proves
Live tests only after dead tests pass; results recorded

essays.stem: Explain how earthing and bonding are arranged in an installation, from the earth electrode to the circuits, and how you would check them.
essays.modelAnswer: The earth electrode, usually an earth rod, is driven into the ground and joined by a clamp to the main earthing conductor, which runs to the main earth terminal or bar at the main board. Main bonding conductors join metal water pipes, gas pipes and other metal services to the main earth terminal, so they stay at the same potential in a fault. From the earth bar, each circuit has its own earth conductor running to every outlet, light point and metal enclosure. Metal boxes, conduit and armour are connected to earth too. To check, I look at every connection for a proper clamp or terminal and a label, test continuity of each circuit's earth to every point and of the bonding conductors, and have the earth electrode tested by a competent person with the right instrument.
markingPoints: Earth rod and main earthing conductor to the main earth terminal
Main bonding of metal services, with reason
Circuit earth conductors to every point and metal part
Visual check of clamps, terminals and labels
Continuity tests and electrode test by a competent person

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would plan and supervise the first fix and second fix of the wiring for a small house, including the checks at each stage.
essays.modelAnswer: I start from the drawings and agree positions with the client and the builder. For first fix, I give each team member an area, mark out box positions at the right heights, and make sure cables run straight up or across from boxes, are fixed and protected, and are labelled at the board end. Before plastering I hold an inspection: I check routes, box fixing, cable sizes and labels, take photos and update the drawing, and only then tell the plasterers to go ahead. For second fix, the team terminates accessories and the board, with the board isolated and locked off. I check samples of every person's terminations, then the team does the dead tests and records them. I correct faults on the spot and explain why. Finally I check labelling, covers and cleanliness before the circuits are energised.
markingPoints: Plans from drawings and coordinates with client and builder
First fix: marked positions, straight routes, fixing and labels
Inspection and records before plastering
Second fix with isolation; checks each person's work
Dead tests recorded, faults corrected, final checks before energising

essays.stem: Explain how Jamaica's climate and site conditions (heat, strong sun, heavy rain, salt air, rodents and termites) affect the choice and installation of wiring systems.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat in roof spaces under zinc or concrete roofs lowers how much current a cable can carry, so correction factors are applied and cables are kept away from the hottest areas where possible. Strong sun breaks down ordinary PVC, so cables and conduit outdoors must be rated for sunlight or protected. Heavy rain and flooding need weatherproof enclosures, drip loops, sealed glands and boards mounted above flood level, with outdoor outlets protected by GFCIs. Salt air near the coast corrodes terminals and steel fittings, so corrosion-resistant or plastic fittings and sealed enclosures are used. Rodents and termites can chew cables, so conduit or trunking and sealed entries help protect them. Underground cables are buried at the right depth with warning tape and protected where they rise.
markingPoints: Heat: correction factors and routing
Sunlight: UV-rated or protected materials
Rain and flooding: weatherproofing, sealed entries, GFCI
Salt air: corrosion-resistant fittings
Rodents and termites: mechanical protection (and buried cable care)

essays.stem: Describe what makes a good termination at a screw terminal, at a busbar lug and at a crimped connection, and explain the faults that cause terminations to overheat.
essays.modelAnswer: At a screw terminal, the conductor is stripped to the right length, fully inserted with no bare copper outside and no insulation under the clamp, stranded conductors have ferrules, and the screw is tightened to the maker's torque. At a busbar lug, the lug matches the conductor size and the stud, it is crimped with the right die, the contact faces are clean and flat, and the bolt has the right washers and torque. A crimped connection uses the matching terminal and tool, with the full ratchet cycle and a pull test. Terminations overheat when they are loose, when insulation is trapped under the clamp, when strands are cut off, when the wrong size of lug or terminal is used, when copper and aluminium are mixed without suitable terminals, or when corrosion builds up.
markingPoints: Screw terminal good practice
Busbar lug good practice
Crimped connection good practice
Overheating faults: loose, trapped insulation, cut strands
Wrong size, mixed metals or corrosion

essays.stem: Explain the steps from finishing a new installation to the client using it: final inspection, testing, paperwork, government inspection, connection and hand-over.
essays.modelAnswer: When the work is complete, I carry out a final inspection of the whole installation and put right any faults. The team carries out and records the dead tests, then the live tests once the supply is available, and the results go on a test certificate signed by the competent person. The circuit chart is completed and fixed in the board, and the drawings are updated to as-built. The installation is then offered for the government electrical inspection, and any defects the inspector finds are corrected. After it passes, the power company can connect the supply and fit the meter; we do not touch their equipment. Finally I hand over to the client: I explain the main switch, the breakers and GFCIs and how to test them, give them the certificate, chart and drawings, and have the job signed off.
markingPoints: Final inspection and corrections
Tests recorded on a certificate
Circuit chart and as-built drawings
Government inspection before the power company connects
Hand-over explanation and documents

essays.stem: Explain how to add a new circuit to an existing board in an occupied building safely, including checking spare capacity, isolating the board and updating the records.
essays.modelAnswer: I first check the board schedule and measure the existing load, to be sure the board and its supply have spare capacity and a spare way for the new breaker. I agree a shutdown time with the occupants, because the whole board must be dead to work inside it safely. On the day I isolate the board at its supply, lock off and tag it, and prove it dead at the busbars and incoming terminals with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after, remembering that the supply side of a main switch may still be live. I fit the breaker, connect the earth, neutral and line in turn, dress the conductors and torque the terminals. I check nothing is left inside, refit covers and blanks, test, then re-energise with everyone informed. Finally I update the circuit chart and test records.
markingPoints: Checks spare capacity and a spare way
Agrees a shutdown with occupants
Isolate, lock off, tag, prove dead with tester checked before and after; aware of live supply side
Correct connection, dressing, torque and tool check
Tests, re-energises safely and updates records

practical1.title: Install, terminate and test a submain and sub-board on a training bay
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a layout for a training bay: a short armoured (or sheathed) submain from a training main board to a small sub-board, which feeds one lighting circuit and one outlet circuit. As a group, plan the job: work out the design currents, choose the breaker and cable sizes from the tables the assessor gives, and check the volt drop. Then install it. The training main board is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after. Each member does at least one main task: glanding and terminating the submain at one end, fixing the sub-board, or installing and terminating one final circuit. The group carries out the visual inspection and dead tests (earth continuity, insulation resistance and polarity) and records them; the assessor energises the bay for any live test. Hand in the calculations, test sheet and an updated circuit chart. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training main board and sub-board with lock-off points
Armoured or sheathed submain cable, glands and lugs
Cable and accessories for one lighting and one outlet circuit
Breakers to suit, labels and circuit chart
Cable tables (rating, correction factors and volt drop) from the assessor
Insulated hand tools, crimpers and torque screwdriver
Voltage tester, proving unit, continuity and insulation resistance tester, test sheet
photos: The calculation sheet for the design currents, cable sizes and volt drop
The main board locked off and tagged, with the tester on the proving unit
The submain gland and armour termination
Inside the sub-board, conductors dressed and labelled
Final circuit terminations at an accessory
The completed test sheet and circuit chart
checklist: Worked out design current, cable size and volt drop correctly
Followed safe isolation with a tester checked before and after
Glanded and terminated the submain with the armour earthed
Dressed, identified and torqued conductors correctly
Installed final circuits neatly with correct polarity
Carried out and recorded the dead tests correctly
Updated the circuit chart and left the bay tidy
safety: Work only on the isolated, locked-off and tagged training boards
Only the person who fitted a lock removes it
Wear safety glasses when cutting armour and stripping cables
Only the assessor energises the bay, with everyone clear

practical2.title: Wire, balance, test and certify the final circuits of a small 110/220 V installation
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group the layout for a training booth set up as a small home: a two-way lighting circuit, two 110 V outlet circuits (one with GFCI protection for an outside outlet in a weatherproof box) and one 220 V appliance circuit on a two-pole breaker. As a group, list the loads, share the 110 V circuits across the two lines of the training board so they are balanced, and draw the circuit chart. Then wire the circuits in conduit or trunking, terminate the accessories and the board, and inspect and dead test every circuit. Each member installs and terminates at least one circuit and tests another member's circuit. The training board is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead throughout; the assessor carries out any live and GFCI tests. Complete a simple installation certificate and hand the booth over to the assessor as the client. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training booth and training board with lock-off point
Conduit or trunking, boxes and fixings
Cable, two-way switches, lamp holders, outlets, weatherproof box and cover
Single-pole, two-pole and GFCI breakers or devices
Insulated hand tools, strippers, crimpers and torque screwdriver
Voltage tester, proving unit, continuity and insulation resistance tester
Load list, circuit chart, test sheet and installation certificate forms
photos: The load list and the balanced circuit chart
The board locked off and tagged, with the tester on the proving unit
Conduit or trunking runs and boxes fixed
Terminations inside the board, with the 220 V circuit on a two-pole breaker
The outside outlet in its weatherproof box
The completed certificate and hand-over to the assessor
checklist: Shared the 110 V loads across both lines sensibly
Followed safe isolation with a tester checked before and after
Installed conduit or trunking and boxes neatly and securely
Connected two-way switching, outlets and the 220 V circuit correctly
Used a two-pole breaker for the 220 V circuit and fitted the GFCI correctly
Carried out and recorded the dead tests
Completed the certificate and explained the installation at hand-over
safety: Never work on a live board; keep it locked off and tagged
Check the tester on the proving unit before and after proving dead
Disconnect any electronic devices before insulation testing
Only the assessor energises the booth for live and GFCI tests
